justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline across the three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 90.5 is anchored closely to what I understood to be the prevailing price or index level at the time of the forecast, with only minimal drift expected over such a short window. For one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 91.0, reflecting a mild positive trend bias and the assumption that near-term momentum or fundamental support would persist without major reversal. By one month, the estimate rises further to 92.0, incorporating a longer-run drift assumption consistent with modest underlying growth or mean-reversion toward a perceived fair value. In all three cases, the point estimates are relatively conservative and do not assume any dramatic directional move.

The confidence interval widths widen significantly as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans just 6 points, consistent with typical daily volatility in a moderately liquid asset or index. By one week, the interval widens to 12 points, accounting for the possibility of several consecutive adverse or favorable sessions accumulating. At one month, the interval expands to 24 points, reflecting the much larger range of plausible macroeconomic developments, sentiment shifts, and technical moves that can materialize over four weeks. The asymmetry in the intervals is relatively mild, suggesting I did not have a strong skew view at the time.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift, or a geopolitical shock could drive the value well below 87.5 even within a single day. Liquidity crises or correlated selling across asset classes are historically fat-tail events that standard volatility-based intervals tend to understate. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst such as a major policy stimulus announcement, a breakthrough earnings report, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could push values above 104 at the one-month horizon. These tail risks are real and serve as a reminder that even 90% confidence intervals leave a meaningful 10% probability mass in the tails, and actual outcomes in financial markets tend to have heavier tails than normal distributions imply.
